title: Maharaja Ranjit Singh
hook: he unites Punjab in 1799 and covers the Harmandir in gold, giving it the name the world knows

segments.voice: Yesterday, the misls: twelve, and one. Today, the young leader from one of those twelve who made them one kingdom.

A shining building sits in the middle of a still pool, its upper walls and dome glowing gold, reflected upside down in the water. Pilgrims walk around it barefoot, day and night. Photos of it hang on kitchen walls and glow on phone screens around the world. But it didn't always look like that. For generations it stood in brick and stone. The gold came later, from a king. Today: Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
screen: `A SHINING BUILDING IN A STILL POOL.` → `ON WALLS AND PHONES WORLDWIDE.` → `THE GOLD CAME LATER.`

segments.voice: Ranjit Singh was born in 1780, the son of the leader of the Sukerchakia misl. As a small child he survived smallpox, which left him blind in one eye. He became chief as a boy, and in 1799, still a young man, he rode into Lahore and took the city. Over the next years he brought the misls and much of the land around them under one rule, and in 1801 he was proclaimed Maharaja, great king, of Punjab. He ruled for almost forty years, until his death in 1839. His was a Sikh kingdom, but not only for Sikhs. Muslims and Hindus served at the top of his government; his foreign minister was a Muslim scholar. Then there's the gold. Ranjit Singh gave generously to many places of worship, and above all to the Harmandir in Amritsar, the temple the Afghans had destroyed and the Sikhs had rebuilt. Over years of work, its upper stories were covered in gilded copper, with inlaid marble added below. English-speaking visitors called it the Golden Temple, and the name stuck. Sikhs usually call it Harmandir Sahib, the house of God, or Darbar Sahib, the Guru's court. Sikhs love to tell one story about him. Accused once of breaking the Sikh code, the Maharaja was summoned before the Akal Takht, and he went, bowed, and accepted its judgment like any other Sikh. Remember the two flags at the Akal Takht, the flag of the spirit standing a little higher? That day, the king took his place beneath it.
screen: `SUKERCHAKIA MISL, BORN 1780.` · `LAHORE 1799, MAHARAJA 1801.` · `GOLD FOR THE HARMANDIR.` · `A KING WHO BOWED TO THE AKAL TAKHT.` · then, large: `THE GOLDEN TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Pick something plain near you, a mug, a chair, a window, your own hands, and look at it the way pilgrims look at the Golden Temple: slowly, as if it were precious. Where did it come from? Who made it, and what has it done for you? Let it shine a little in your attention, without changing anything about it.
Maharaja. Great king — the title taken by Ranjit Singh in 1801, the Sikh king who united Punjab, covered the Harmandir in gold, and still bowed to the Akal Takht.
Your line: the golden temple. Gold on the walls, and a king who still bowed. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh as the ruler of the Sikh Empire; his samadhi stands in Lahore, and the gilding he gave to Harmandir Sahib, which Sikhs often call Darbar Sahib, is renewed and cared for to this day.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Harmandir Sahib, the house of God (Hari); the world calls it the Golden Temple.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Golden Temple was always golden.
what it means: a king's gift of gold to a rebuilt temple, which gave it the name the world knows.

what a scholar hears: the gilding of the upper stories with gilded copper plates was done over years in the early nineteenth century; the story of his summons to the Akal Takht, often linked to Akali Phula Singh, is traditional.

notes: Taking of Lahore dated July 1799; proclamation as Maharaja 1801 (Vaisakhi); death 1839. Confirm.
Foreign minister Fakir Azizuddin (unnamed in script); confirm.
The Akal Takht summons story (often with Akali Phula Singh and a sentence of flogging later remitted) is traditional; framed as 'a story Sikhs love to tell'.
Exact dates of the gilding (begun about 1802, much of it in the 1830s) are left general.

Review (fresh editor): hook no longer opens 'Ask almost anyone to picture'; 'for most of its history' was wrong (built c. 1604, gilded from c. 1802, so roughly half); Ranjit Singh (born Nov 1780) was 18, not 19, when he took Lahore in July 1799, so the age is cut from the teach and the match pair; the claim that British visitors coined 'Golden Temple' softened; the garbled two-flags line rewritten; 'most Sikhs' softened.
